newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria cabinet considers currency board - premier.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria cabinet considers currency board - premier.

text.p: Bulgaria's cabinet is giving serious consideration to pegging the lev through a currency board as one option for restoring confidence in the tumbling currency, Prime Minister Zhan Videnov said on Friday.

"The IMF proposal to establish a currency board in Bulgaria was seriously discussed by the cabinet yesterday and there was a conclusion that it offers an alternative for restoring confidence in the banking sphere," Videnov told reporters at Sofia airport before leaving for Austria.
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) says a currency board would stabilise the lev, curb inflation and boost economic growth.
Videnov said the other option was maintaining high interest rates, currently at 180 percent a year.
Currency boards, pegging the local currency usually to the dollar, have been used by Argentina, Estonia, Lithuania and Latvia to restore confidence and help defeat hyperinflation.
The central bank must back local currency in circulation with foreign currency, gold reserves or bonds.
On Wednesday, the Bulgarian National Bank said it opposed the proposal, calling it "a risky experiment".
But Finance Minister Dimitar Kostov said on Thursday he believed a currency board was the less risky of the two and a political consensus was needed on which option to choose.
The lev eased to 251.50-252.50 per dollar in early Friday trade from Thursday's 250-251.50 close on newspaper reports that the IMF might suspend funding unless Bulgaria agreed to a currency board.
An IMF mission currently in Sofia is discussing terms for release of a twice-delayed $115 million credit, vital if Bulgaria is to avoid default on its $10 billion foreign debt.
Kostov said a currency board would require amendment of several laws which would deprive the central bank of the usual tools of monetary management, such as market interventions and interest rates.
The central bank would completely stop funding the budget deficit and refinancing of commercial banks would be drastically reduced.

Kostov said the amount of levs in circulation, including commercial banks' minimum reserve deposits in the central bank, totalling 169 billion levs would have to be matched with the country's foreign exchange reserves.

BNB forex reserves stood at $541 million at the end of October and the country would also have to collateralise its gold, said Kostov. He did not elaborate on whether all of the country's gold would be collateralised or only some 4.5 tonnes kept in banks abroad.
